{{Short description|Maximal connected Abelian subgroup}}
{{For|a Cartan subgroup of a Lie group|Cartan subalgebra#Cartan subgroup}}

In the theory of [[algebraic group]]s, a '''Cartan subgroup''' of a connected [[linear algebraic group]] <math>G</math> over a (not necessarily algebraically closed) field <math>k</math> is the centralizer of a maximal torus. Cartan subgroups are smooth (equivalently reduced), connected and nilpotent. If <math>k</math> is algebraically closed, they are all conjugate to each other. {{sfnp|Milne|2017|loc=Proposition 17.44}}

Notice that in the context of algebraic groups a ''torus'' is an algebraic group <math>T</math>
such that the base extension <math>T_{(\bar{k})}</math> (where <math>\bar{k}</math> is the algebraic closure of <math>k</math>) is isomorphic to the product of a finite number of copies of the <math>\mathbf{G}_m=\mathbf{GL}_1</math>. Maximal such subgroups have in the theory of algebraic groups a role that is similar to that of [[maximal torus|maximal tori]] in the theory of [[Lie group]]s.

If <math>G</math> is [[reductive group|reductive]] (in particular, if it is semi-simple), then a torus is maximal if and only if it is its own centraliser {{sfnp|Milne|2017|loc=Corollary 17.84}} and thus Cartan subgroups of <math>G</math> are precisely the maximal tori.

== Example ==
The general linear groups <math>\mathbf{GL}_n</math> are reductive. The diagonal subgroup is clearly a torus (indeed a ''split'' torus, since it is product of n copies of <math>\mathbf{G}_m</math> already before any base extension), and it can be shown to be maximal. Since <math>\mathbf{GL}_n</math> is reductive, the diagonal subgroup is a Cartan subgroup.
